quotes.t: Everyone always talks about a good thing coming to an end, as if life was over.
They hate you if you're clever, and they despise a fool.

I'm not claiming divinity. I've never claimed purity of soul. I've never claimed to have the answers to life. I only put out songs and answer questions as honestly as I can… But I still believe in peace, love and understanding.
Democracy substitutes election by the incompetent many for appointment by the corrupt few.
If history repeats itself, and the unexpected always happens, how incapable must Man be of learning from experience!
Marriage is popular because it combines the maximum of temptation with the maximum of opportunity.
These laws weren't made now or yesterday. They live for all time.
The mind that is most rigid stumbles soonest; the hardest iron — tempered in fire till it is super-strong — shatters easily and clatters into shards.
No man could frighten me into taking on the gods' penalty for breaking such a law.
The man who has become a thinking being feels a compulsion to give every will-to-live the same reverence for life that he gives to his own. He experiences that other life in his own.

The great fault of all ethics hitherto has been that they believed themselves to have to deal only with the relations of man to man. In reality, however, the question is what is his attitude to the world and all life that comes within his reach.
quotes.source: Out of My Life and Thought (1933)

quotes.t: Affirmation of the world, which means affirmation of the will-to-live that manifests itself around me, is only possible if I devote myself to other life.
Death is nothing, but to live defeated and inglorious is to die daily.
The true conquests, the only ones that cause no regrets, are those made over ignorance.
All great events hang always only by a hair.
We hold on to hope, and hope robs us of the present moment.
The most important aspect of being on a spiritual path may be to just keep moving.
Ego could be defined as whatever covers up basic goodness.
With time and patience the mulberry leaf becomes a silk gown.
Your teacher can open the door, but you must enter by yourself.
Do not remove a fly from your friend's forehead with a hatchet.
Each moment is all being, is the entire world.
Students today should begrudge every moment of time. This dewlike life fades away; time speeds swiftly. In this short life of ours, avoid involvement in superfluous things and just study the Way.
Right and wrong are temporal, but time is neither right nor wrong.
I would rather sit on a pumpkin and have it all to myself, than be crowded on a velvet cushion.
Live in each season as it passes; breathe the air, drink the drink, taste the fruit, and resign yourself to the influence of the earth.
In Wildness is the preservation of the World.
To fear death, gentlemen, is no other than to think oneself wise when one is not, to think one knows what one does not know.
I shall obey God rather than you, and while I have life and strength I shall never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy.
Our greatest blessings come to us by way of madness, provided the madness is given us by divine gift.
History is almost always written by the victors and conquerors and gives their view.
Peace is not a relationship of nations. It is a condition of mind brought about by a serenity of soul.
Freedom and power bring responsibility.
He who commits injustice is ever made more wretched than he who suffers it.
Wealth is the parent of luxury and indolence, and poverty of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent.
The soul takes nothing with her to the next world but her education and her culture.
I have never made but one prayer to God, a very short one: O Lord, make my enemies ridiculous! And God granted it.
quotes.source: Letter to Étienne Noël Damilaville, 16 May 1767

quotes.t: If this is the best of all possible worlds, what are the others?
In general, the art of government consists in taking as much money as possible from one part of the citizens to give to the other.
There never was a good war or a bad peace.
Love your enemies, for they tell you your faults.
He that lives upon hope will die fasting.
I loved her against reason, against promise, against peace, against hope, against happiness, against all discouragement that could be.
Vices are sometimes only virtues carried to excess!
There are books of which the backs and covers are by far the best parts.
I'm Nobody! Who are you?
After great pain, a formal feeling comes —
quotes.source: After great pain, a formal feeling comes (Poem 341)

quotes.t: I heard a Fly buzz — when I died —
quotes.source: I heard a Fly buzz — when I died (Poem 465)

quotes.t: The function of education is to teach one to think intensively and to think critically.
If it falls to your lot to be a street sweeper, sweep streets like Michelangelo painted pictures.
If a man hasn't discovered something that he will die for, he isn't fit to live.
A lady's imagination is very rapid; it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony, in a moment.
To sit in the shade on a fine day, and look upon verdure, is the most perfect refreshment.
I wish, as well as everybody else, to be perfectly happy; but, like everybody else, it must be in my own way.
Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly.
quotes.source: War and Peace, Book IV, Ch. 11

quotes.t: A man is like a fraction whose numerator is what he is and whose denominator is what he thinks of himself. The larger the denominator, the smaller the fraction.
But art is not a handicraft; it is the transmission of feeling the artist has experienced.
Is the world to go to pot, or am I to go without my tea? I say that the world may go to pot for me so long as I always get my tea.

Man is a mystery. It must be unraveled, and if you spend your whole life unraveling it, do not say that you have wasted your time; I occupy myself with this mystery because I want to be a human being.
To be a man among people and remain a man for ever, not to be downhearted nor to fall in whatever misfortunes may befall me — this is life; this is the task of life.
People living deeply have no fear of death.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 2 (1934–1939)

quotes.t: I know what I want, I have a goal, an opinion, I have a religion and love. Let me be myself and then I am satisfied.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (11 April 1944)

quotes.t: To forgive is not just to be altruistic. It is the best form of self-interest.
Poverty is the lack of many things, but avarice is the lack of all things.
The greatest of faults, I should say, is to be conscious of none.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841)

quotes.t: I thought how unpleasant it is to be locked out; and I thought how it is worse, perhaps, to be locked in.
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness.

I do know that for the sympathy of one living being, I would make peace with all. I have love in me the likes of which you can scarcely imagine and rage the likes of which you would not believe. If I cannot satisfy the one, I will indulge the other.
I want to put a ding in the universe.
Constitution is not a mere lawyers' document, it is a vehicle of Life, and its spirit is always the spirit of Age.
quotes.source: Speech to the Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

quotes.t: The object of teaching a child is to enable him to get along without his teacher.
The constant assertion of belief is an indication of fear.
I hold it that a little rebellion now and then is a good thing, and as necessary in the political world as storms in the physical.
Warm, eager, living life — to be rooted in life — to learn, to desire to know, to feel, to think, to act. That is what I want. And nothing less.
quotes.source: The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (10 October 1922)

quotes.t: You will go most safely in the middle.
I try to avoid looking forward or backward, and try to keep looking upward.
The safety of the people shall be the highest law.
Wherever you are, be there totally.
The thing worse than rebellion is the thing that causes rebellion.
The person who tries to live alone will not succeed as a human being. His heart withers if it does not answer another heart.
I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey work of the stars.
What can we do? We must live our lives.
When we change, the world changes.
The fight is won or lost far away from witnesses — behind the lines, in the gym, and out there on the road, long before I dance under those lights.
You can get everything in life you want if you will just help enough other people get what they want.
Don't panic.
quotes.source: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1979)

quotes.t: Ah, but a man's reach should exceed his grasp, or what's a heaven for?
We must love one another or die.
Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
Each generation must discover its mission, fulfill it or betray it, in relative opacity.
Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts.
We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
The only way of discovering the limits of the possible is to venture a little way past them into the impossible.
Men are free when they are in a living homeland, not when they are straying and breaking away.
I have made a ceaseless effort not to ridicule, not to bewail, not to scorn human actions, but to understand them.
quotes.source: A Political Treatise (Tractatus Politicus), Ch. I, §4 (1677)

quotes.t: To learn which questions are unanswerable, and not to answer them: this skill is most needful in times of stress and darkness.
Instructions for living a life. Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it.
Thou hast made us for thyself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it finds its rest in thee.
I would rather drudge out my life on a cotton plantation, till the grave opened to give me rest, than to live with an unprincipled master and a jealous mistress.
quotes.source: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Ch. VI (1861)

quotes.t: Get busy living, or get busy dying.
quotes.source: "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption", Different Seasons (1982)

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Arthur C. Clarke.bio: British science-fiction writer (1917–2008), author of 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Augustine of Hippo.bio: Saint Augustine of Hippo, one of the most influential thinkers in Western Christianity. His Confessions and The City of God shaped theology and philosophy for more than a thousand years.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Baruch Spinoza.bio: Baruch Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent who ground lenses for a living while writing works that reshaped philosophy. Expelled from his synagogue for his views, he argued in the Ethics for a rational, pantheistic understanding of God and nature.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

D.H. Lawrence.bio: English novelist and poet (1885–1930), author of Sons and Lovers and Lady Chatterley's Lover.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Douglas Adams.bio: Douglas Adams was an English author best known for The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, which began as a BBC radio comedy and became a series of bestselling books. He also wrote the Dirk Gently detective novels.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frantz Fanon.bio: Martinican psychiatrist and philosopher whose books Black Skin, White Masks and The Wretched of the Earth became foundational texts on colonialism, race and liberation. He joined Algeria's independence struggle and died at thirty-six.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Harriet Jacobs.bio: American abolitionist and writer (1813–1897), author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861), the first full-length narrative by a Black woman published in the United States.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Joan Didion.bio: Joan Didion was an American writer and journalist famed for her cool, precise prose in essays like Slouching Towards Bethlehem and the memoir The Year of Magical Thinking, which won the National Book Award.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Oliver.bio: American poet (1935–2019) who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1984 and the National Book Award in 1992, known for her nature poetry.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Rachel Carson.bio: Rachel Carson was an American marine biologist and conservationist whose book Silent Spring (1962) exposed the dangers of synthetic pesticides and is credited with advancing the modern environmental movement.

Robert Browning.bio: Robert Browning was an English poet famed for his dramatic monologues, in which speakers reveal themselves in their own words. Married to the poet Elizabeth Barrett, he spent much of his life in Italy and published his masterpiece, The Ring and the Book, in 1868-69.

Simone Weil.bio: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic and political activist. Her posthumously published works, including Gravity and Grace and The Need for Roots, combine rigorous thought with deep spiritual and social concern.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Stephen King.bio: Stephen King (born 1947) is an American author of horror and supernatural fiction whose bestselling novels include Carrie, The Shining, and It.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Ursula K. Le Guin.bio: Ursula K. Le Guin (1929–2018) was an American author of science fiction and fantasy, known for A Wizard of Earthsea, The Left Hand of Darkness, and The Dispossessed.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

W. H. Auden.bio: W. H. Auden was an English-American poet regarded as one of the greatest writers of the twentieth century, author of poems such as 'Funeral Blues' and 'Musée des Beaux Arts'. His work ranges across politics, love, religion and psychology in a dazzling variety of forms.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
